article_title: Talent Development High School (TDHS) — Strategic Reading and Student Team Literature
citation: Talent Development High School. (2004). Talent Development High School program description and evidence review. https://www.bestevidence.org
title: Double-dose semester block: Strategic Reading first semester, English 1 second semester
description: TDHS gives ninth graders a double dose of reading: students take double periods of Strategic Reading, 90 minutes daily, in the first semester, and then double periods of English 1 in the second semester. This sequencing concentrates intensive reading instruction before the standard English course. The pattern is the structural backbone of the reading component of the whole-school model.
requirements: Scheduling capacity for 90-minute daily double reading periods in the first semester
constraints: Applies to ninth graders in high-poverty schools as implemented in the qualifying study
target_learners: Ninth graders in high-poverty high schools
examples: Double periods of Strategic Reading (90 minutes daily) in the first semester, then double periods of English 1 in the second semester
key_sources: Talent Development High School. (2004). Talent Development High School program description and evidence review. https://www.bestevidence.org

article_title: Talent Development High School (TDHS) — Strategic Reading and Student Team Literature
citation: Talent Development High School. (2004). Talent Development High School program description and evidence review. https://www.bestevidence.org
title: Cooperative learning groups with paired reading, vocabulary practice, and structured partner discussion guides
description: In Strategic Reading, students work in small, interdependent cooperative learning groups. Activities include paired reading for fluency and comprehension, practice with new vocabulary related to novels and plays, and structured partner discussion guides that provide background, vocabulary, and comprehension questions to help students identify characters, plots, and informational content. Students also get time for self-selected reading and writing activities.
requirements: Structured partner discussion guides providing background, vocabulary, and comprehension questions
High-quality student materials, which teachers unanimously rated highly in the implementation survey
target_learners: Ninth graders in high-poverty high schools
target_learning_goals: Comprehension of characters, plots, and informational content
examples: Paired reading for fluency and comprehension; mini-lessons on specific comprehension strategies; self-selected reading and writing activities
key_sources: Talent Development High School. (2004). Talent Development High School program description and evidence review. https://www.bestevidence.org

article_title: Talent Development High School (TDHS) — Strategic Reading and Student Team Literature
citation: Talent Development High School. (2004). Talent Development High School program description and evidence review. https://www.bestevidence.org
title: Support whole-school reading reform with sustained job-embedded coaching rather than one-off training
description: The program's implementation model pairs brief start-up training with sustained job-embedded support: two days of start-up and awareness training for all Strategic Reading teachers, plus two days per month of job-embedded JHU Instructional Facilitator support, within roughly 20 days of facilitator support overall. A minimum of 3 days of technical assistance from a JHU ELA facilitator is required. Teachers rated the in-class assistance and workshop training highly.
requirements: One FTE English teacher per cohort of 75-100 students; an English Instructional Coach if possible
constraints: A minimum of 3 days of technical assistance from a JHU ELA facilitator is required
target_learners: Ninth graders in high-poverty high schools
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and fluency through well-implemented Strategic Reading
examples: Two days per month of job-embedded JHU Instructional Facilitator support during 2002-2003 implementation
key_sources: Talent Development High School. (2004). Talent Development High School program description and evidence review. https://www.bestevidence.org

article_title: Test-Driven, AI-Assisted Learning: Replacing Lectures with Weekly Closed-Book Tests
citation: Jin-Guo Liu, Shang-Qi Lu, Xin-Ran Shi, Long-Li Zheng, Wei Wang. (2026). Test-Driven, AI-Assisted Learning: Replacing Lectures with Weekly Closed-Book Tests. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23315
title: TDAA: high-frequency closed-book tests paired with a human-reviewed AI production harness
description: TDAA is a course-level design pattern coupling two cycles: students prepare with aligned materials and face a weekly closed-book gate, while an instructor-side AI harness drafts, reviews, and grades the materials under human approval. The paper states the pairing directly: "high-frequency tests preserve individual accountability, while AI agents make material production and marking scalable." Without the agent layer weekly testing is infeasible for one instructor; without the test gate AI-assisted preparation offers no reliable check on unaided performance.
requirements: A visible preparation path of learning sheets and aligned validation practice so the closed-book tests feel fair rather than arbitrary
A version-controlled agent workspace with human review before any AI draft reaches students
constraints: Evidence is limited to one small, proof-heavy course without a control group; transfer to large or non-proof courses is a hypothesis for future offerings, not a result
target_learners: upper-level undergraduate data-science students in a proof-heavy course
target_learning_goals: unaided problem-solving and proof-writing in theory of computation
examples: DSAA 3071 ran 13 weeks with a 30-minute closed-book test, 120-minute self-paced study block, and 20-minute discussion each week, with 30% weekly tests and 70% final exam
key_sources: Jin-Guo Liu, Shang-Qi Lu, Xin-Ran Shi, Long-Li Zheng, Wei Wang. (2026). Test-Driven, AI-Assisted Learning: Replacing Lectures with Weekly Closed-Book Tests. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23315

article_title: Test-Driven, AI-Assisted Learning: Replacing Lectures with Weekly Closed-Book Tests
citation: Jin-Guo Liu, Shang-Qi Lu, Xin-Ran Shi, Long-Li Zheng, Wei Wang. (2026). Test-Driven, AI-Assisted Learning: Replacing Lectures with Weekly Closed-Book Tests. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23315
title: Public TDAA starter-template harness for AI-assisted course production
description: A released, reusable course-materials harness: a version-controlled workspace where AI agents draft, cross-check, build, write grading rubrics, and mark first passes, while the instructor reviews, repairs, and approves. The authors "release the reusable harness as a public starter template, separate from the course-specific content", bundling document and website templates, build commands, a GitHub Pages workflow, and named AI-assisted skills so another instructor can bootstrap a course and run AI-assisted grading.
requirements: A version-controlled text workspace where AI output is inspectable, rebuildable, and constrained by named skills
constraints: The textbook knowledge base was converted from a licensed copy and used only as a private, instructor-side reference, not part of the public release
target_learning_goals: producing and grading aligned weekly course materials at scale
examples: The harness surrounded the agent with a project specification, a knowledge base, tools such as Grep and Git, and named skills for drafting, reviewing, and grading
key_sources: Jin-Guo Liu, Shang-Qi Lu, Xin-Ran Shi, Long-Li Zheng, Wei Wang. (2026). Test-Driven, AI-Assisted Learning: Replacing Lectures with Weekly Closed-Book Tests. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23315

article_title: Transcranial direct current stimulation targeting the bilateral IFG alters cognitive processes during creative ideation
citation: Xie, C., Zhang, S., Qiao, X., & Hao, N. (2024). Transcranial direct current stimulation targeting the bilateral IFG alters cognitive processes during creative ideation. npj Science of Learning, 9, 75. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00285-z
title: Compensation account: tDCS can modify creative cognition itself rather than merely enhancing or inhibiting it
description: The article proposes that brain stimulation may not simply raise or lower a fixed creative process but can reorganize it: "the effects of tDCS might extend beyondmere enhancement or inhibition of certain cognitive functions; it could also lead to a modiﬁcation of creative cognition itself". Drawing on compensation research, it posits that if associative processes are disrupted, executive processes may compensate, weakening the correlation between associative ability and creativity without necessarily lowering creativity. The CRA and EEG-classification results are read through this lens: L+R− stimulation shifted solving toward analytical strategies and L−R+ toward remote associations, while overall performance stayed comparable across groups.
requirements: Requires a convergent-thinking task with trial-level semantic metrics (e.g., CRA with quantified relative semantic distance) plus task-related neural recording to detect process shifts that overall performance measures miss.
constraints: Demonstrated at the group level for one 15-min 1.5 mA tDCS protocol pair over F7/F8 during a Chinese-language CRA task; the authors note individual differences in tDCS effects were not analyzed.
EEG's relatively low spatial resolution and decision-tree classifiers limit inference about activation of specific brain areas, per the article's stated limitations.
target_learning_goals: understanding how neural stimulation changes creative cognitive processes
examples: Participants were randomly assigned to L+R−, L−R+, or Sham tDCS before a Stroop task and a 20-trial Chinese CRA task with EEG recorded, and 80 functional-connectivity classification models were built per group per frequency band.
key_sources: Xie, C., Zhang, S., Qiao, X., & Hao, N. (2024). Transcranial direct current stimulation targeting the bilateral IFG alters cognitive processes during creative ideation. npj Science of Learning, 9, 75. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00285-z

article_title: From digital literacy to digital competence: the teacher digital competency (TDC) framework
citation: Garry Falloon. (2020). From digital literacy to digital competence: the teacher digital competency (TDC) framework. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09767-4
title: The Teacher Digital Competence (TDC) framework integrates curriculum, personal-ethical and personal-professional competencies
description: The TDC framework is a conceptual framework depicting broadly-based teacher digital competence as three integrated competency sets. It extends TPACK-aligned curriculum competencies (technical, technological, discipline/content, pedagogical/learning design) with personal-ethical pillars (digital citizenship, safety and data security, health and wellbeing, impacts on people, society and environment) and personal-professional pillars (information literacy, strategic professional networking, commitment to continuous professional learning). The article states the framework 'represents diagrammatically a broadly-based conceptualisation of teacher digital competence', with double-headed arrows indicating the interrelated nature of the pillars. It is intended to inform curriculum and programme design in teacher education rather than prescribe content.
requirements: All teaching faculty must have a consistent understanding of the breadth and definition of the competencies for successful implementation
Targeted TDC elements should be made explicit to students via course outlines, integrated into course content, and reflected in assessment tasks
constraints: The article states conceptual frameworks are not intended to act as a formula or prescription detailing universally-applicable curricula; content must be tailored by expert professionals to context
The discussion and suggestions for use specifically focus on applicability to teacher education, though it could equally inform practicing teachers
target_learners: pre-service teachers in initial teacher education programmes
target_learning_goals: digital competence for using digital technologies safely, ethically and productively in teaching
examples: Health education faculty integrating personal-ethical (wellbeing/safety) competencies by requiring students to research effects of prolonged device use; science education courses aligning with information access competencies through scientific networks
key_sources: Garry Falloon. (2020). From digital literacy to digital competence: the teacher digital competency (TDC) framework. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09767-4

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of School-Based Interventions Aimed to Prevent or Reduce Violence in Teen Dating Relationships
citation: Lisa De La Rue, Joshua R. Polanin, Dorothy L. Espelage, Terri D. Pigott. (2017). A Meta-Analysis of School-Based Interventions Aimed to Prevent or Reduce Violence in Teen Dating Relationships. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654316632061
title: Dating violence prevention programs should explicitly incorporate skill-building components to promote behavior change
description: The article recommends that future dating violence prevention interventions explicitly include skill-building components, because knowledge and attitude change alone are unlikely to change behavior. It argues that "without a skill-building component that integrates specific training to modify behavior and develop competencies, it is unlikely that behavior change will be accomplished." Of the included studies, only two clearly described a skill-building component.
requirements: Programs aiming to change perpetration or victimization behavior must include explicit skill-building training, such as practicing how to discuss disagreements and how to leave an abusive relationship or seek support.
constraints: The review found only two included studies clearly described a skill-building component, and the small number of studies limited the ability to differentiate intervention types or components.
target_learners: middle and high school students in Grades 6 to 12, ages 11 to 18
examples: The Safe Dates program includes activities intended to shift dating violence and gender role norms as well as to increase conflict management skills; the Fourth R and Safe Dates studies were the two included studies that clearly described a skill-building component.
key_sources: Lisa De La Rue, Joshua R. Polanin, Dorothy L. Espelage, Terri D. Pigott. (2017). A Meta-Analysis of School-Based Interventions Aimed to Prevent or Reduce Violence in Teen Dating Relationships. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654316632061

article_title: Examining the Effects of Teacher-Directed Opportunities to Respond on Student Outcomes: A Systematic Review of the Literature
citation: MacSuga-Gage, A. S., & Simonsen, B. (2015). Examining the Effects of Teacher-Directed Opportunities to Respond on Student Outcomes: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Education and Treatment of Children, 38(2), 211-240.
title: Teacher-directed opportunities to respond (TD-OTR): antecedent-response-feedback framework with individual and unison modalities
description: The review organizes TD-OTR research around a behavioral definition: "teacher behaviors (i.e., antecedent stimuli) that occasion student responses", followed by teacher feedback contingent on the response. The framework distinguishes two categories of TD-OTRs — teacher-directed individual responses and teacher-directed unison responses (choral, gestural, written, or clicker-based) — and the review uses it to code each included study's modality and delivery rate.
requirements: Requires a teacher delivering prompts during direct instruction and providing feedback contingent on student responses
constraints: Applies to teacher-directed response opportunities only; peer tutoring and other non-teacher-directed OTRs are excluded from the framework's scope
target_learners: K-12 students with and without disabilities in general and special education classrooms
target_learning_goals: Increased academic achievement and positive classroom behavior through active engagement
examples: The review coded all 15 included studies' independent variables using this framework, distinguishing modality comparisons (e.g., response cards, choral responding, SRS) from rate-increasing interventions.
key_sources: MacSuga-Gage, A. S., & Simonsen, B. (2015). Examining the Effects of Teacher-Directed Opportunities to Respond on Student Outcomes: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Education and Treatment of Children, 38(2), 211-240. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1070193

article_title: Barriers and Facilitators to Self-Directed Learning in Continuing Professional Development for Physicians in Canada: A Scoping Review.
citation: Dahn J, Presseau J, ElChamaa R, Naumann DN, Mascaro C, Luconi F, Smith KM, Kitto S. (2018). Barriers and Facilitators to Self-Directed Learning in Continuing Professional Development for Physicians in Canada: A Scoping Review. Academic Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/ACM.0000000000002237
title: Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) for coding SDL behavior-change barriers and facilitators
description: The TDF is, in the article's words, "a comprehensive framework composed of 12 domains that synthesize 128 explanatory constructs drawing on 33 psychological theories associated with clinical behavior change." The review used it as the second step of a two-step analysis, directing coding of charted barriers and facilitators into the 12 domains for two units of analysis: physicians engaging in SDL and SDL developers implementing programs. The authors report this as the first TDF-guided directed coding in a scoping review on SDL in CPD.
requirements: A coding manual based on the 12 TDF domains and coder calibration with a TDF expert to operationalize domains and constructs
constraints: The authors note the TDF process is time-consuming and resource-intensive, and developing interrater understanding of domains was challenging
Key domains were determined by frequency counts, which the authors say do not imply importance
target_learning_goals: identifying barriers and facilitators to self-directed learning engagement and program implementation
examples: The review coded 318 barriers and facilitators from 17 articles into the 12 TDF domains, identifying four key domains
key_sources: Dahn J, Presseau J, ElChamaa R, Naumann DN, Mascaro C, Luconi F, Smith KM, Kitto S. (2018). Barriers and Facilitators to Self-Directed Learning in Continuing Professional Development for Physicians in Canada: A Scoping Review. Academic Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/ACM.0000000000002237

article_title: Effectiveness of PowerPoint Presentation on Students' Cognitive Achievement in Technical Drawing
citation: Amosa Isiaka Gambari, Hamdalat Taiwo Yusuf, Sherifat Adepeju Balogun. (2014). Effectiveness of Powerpoint Presentation On Students' Cognitive Achievement in Technical Drawing. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, Volume 3, Issue 4. http://www.mojet.net
title: Technical Drawing Achievement Test (TDAT)
description: The Technical Drawing Achievement Test (TDAT) is a researcher-developed instrument used to collect achievement data in this study. It has two sections: Section 1 elicited biodata such as school, class, gender and achievement level, and Section 2 is a "25-multiple-choice test items with five options (A-E)". It was validated by experts in Industrial and Technology Education, Basic Technology teachers, and test-and-measurement specialists from NECO, Minna, and was administered as both pretest and posttest.
requirements: Validated by subject and measurement experts before use, as the article describes
constraints: Reliability is reported inconsistently: the abstract gives .88 using KR-20 while the methodology reports .84 using KR-21
target_learning_goals: Technical Drawing concepts in Basic Technology
examples: Administered as pretest to ascertain group equivalence before the four-week treatment, then as posttest to measure achievement in each group

article_title: Thinking, Doing, Talking Science: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Pam Hanley, Robert Slavin, Louise Elliott. (2015). Thinking, Doing, Talking Science: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. http://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN54969918
title: Thinking, Doing, Talking Science (TDTS) professional development programme for primary science
description: TDTS is a primary school CPD programme in which two teachers per school receive five full-day training sessions across a year, designed to make science lessons more conceptually challenging, practical and interactive. It deliberately avoids off-the-shelf lesson plans, instead building a repertoire of strategies including a "dedicated discussion slot, the ‘Bright Ideas Time’" with prompts such as the Odd One Out, the PMI and the Big Question, plus Practical Prompts for Thinking demonstrations. Teachers also get in-school planning time and an equipment and resources package.
requirements: Two teachers per school attend five full days of professional development spread across the academic year, with dedicated in-school planning time to embed the strategies
constraints: The trial was run in a single local authority area (Oxfordshire), so the sample of schools was drawn from a restricted geographical area
examples: In the trial, schools were charged £1,000 each covering five INSET days, a launch day, and resources, at an estimated cost of £26 per pupil; training days were themed around curriculum areas such as evolution, forces and electricity.
key_sources: Pam Hanley, Robert Slavin, Louise Elliott. (2015). Thinking, Doing, Talking Science: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. http://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN54969918

article_title: Pharmacy students' perspectives and training needs on simulation-based interprofessional education at a University in Southwestern Uganda: a qualitative study.
citation: Kyomya Julius, Najjuma Josephine Nambi, Atwiine Fredrick, Lukyamuzi Edward John, Musinguzi Pius, Maleka Emmanuel, Maling Samuel, Muhindo Rose, Wonde Shewatatek Gedamu. (2026). Pharmacy students’ perspectives and training needs on simulation-based interprofessional education at a University in Southwestern Uganda: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09769-5
title: Theoretical Domains Framework as organizing lens for sim-IPE implementation determinants
description: The study used the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF), which "brings together constructs from multiple behavior change theories to help identify factors that influence behavior and implementation." It has 14 domains including knowledge, skills, social/professional role and identity, beliefs about capabilities, beliefs about consequences, environmental context and resources, social influences, emotion, and behavioral regulation. Interview guides and the initial coding matrix were built on TDF domains, while analysis allowed themes to emerge across domains rather than being constrained to the framework structure.
requirements: Implementation of sim-IPE requires changes in learner, faculty, and institutional factors, including readiness to collaborate, confidence, role understanding, motivation, and organizational resources
constraints: Analysis was not restricted to predefined TDF domains; themes emerged across domains
key_sources: Kyomya Julius, Najjuma Josephine Nambi, Atwiine Fredrick, Lukyamuzi Edward John, Musinguzi Pius, Maleka Emmanuel, Maling Samuel, Muhindo Rose, Wonde Shewatatek Gedamu. (2026). Pharmacy students’ perspectives and training needs on simulation-based interprofessional education at a University in Southwestern Uganda: a qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09769-5

article_title: Comparing traditional and online problem-based learning in child and adolescent psychiatry in Nagoya: a novel statistical approach in Japanese educational settings.
citation: Basile, C., Nishida, K., Kondo, T., Takahashi, N., Takami, H., Nishigori, H., Aleksic, B., Dolladille, C., Villalobos, I. B., Yagi, T., Skokauskas, N., & Kasuya, H. (2026). Comparing traditional and online problem-based learning in child and adolescent psychiatry in Nagoya: a novel statistical approach in Japanese educational settings. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09517-9
title: Transactional Distance Theory and Community of Inquiry as explanatory frameworks for online PBL satisfaction
description: The article applies Transactional Distance Theory (TDT), in which educational "distance" is "psychological and pedagogical, determined by the interplay of dialogue, structure, and learner autonomy", alongside the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework requiring social, cognitive and teaching presence. It hypothesises that online environments offer a "safe harbor" reducing transactional distance for Japanese students communicating in English. The authors emphasise these frameworks were compatible with, but not directly tested by, their observational design.
requirements: Effective online PBL requires the intersection of social, cognitive, and teaching presence per the CoI framework
constraints: The study did not directly measure transactional distance, social presence, language anxiety or cognitive load
target_learning_goals: Clinical problem-solving in child and adolescent psychiatry
key_sources: Basile, C., Nishida, K., Kondo, T., Takahashi, N., Takami, H., Nishigori, H., Aleksic, B., Dolladille, C., Villalobos, I. B., Yagi, T., Skokauskas, N., & Kasuya, H. (2026). Comparing traditional and online problem-based learning in child and adolescent psychiatry in Nagoya: a novel statistical approach in Japanese educational settings. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09517-9

article_title: The evaluation of declarative and objective knowledge of first aid for dental traumatic injuries among medical students: development and validation of a competency assessment tool.
citation: Pawlaczyk-Kamieńska T, Jastrzębski B, Kamieńska P, Kamieńska W, Marushko O, Marushko O, Kruszyńska D. (2025). The evaluation of declarative and objective knowledge of first aid for dental traumatic injuries among medical students: development and validation of a competency assessment tool. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08153-z
title: TDI-KNOW Index — a standardized 21-question competency assessment tool for theoretical knowledge of dental trauma first aid
description: The TDI-KNOW Index is an original, standardized instrument for objectively assessing medical students' theoretical knowledge of first aid for dental traumatic injuries. It consists of 21 closed-ended questions covering crown fractures of permanent teeth and tooth avulsion, each scored 0–3 for accuracy and completeness, with the cumulative score (maximum 63 points) converted to a percentage and classified as low (0–49%), medium (50–79%), or high (80–100%). The authors state it "addresses the limitations of earlier studies that used varied and non-standardized surveys" and can serve as both a research tool and a method for evaluating educational interventions.
requirements: Respondents must answer all 21 closed-ended questions for the index to be computed
Scoring is based on current international guidelines for treating dental injuries
constraints: It focuses solely on theoretical knowledge and does not measure practical competencies
Its closed-ended format may not fully capture the complexities of real-world clinical decision-making
Validated only at a single medical faculty; multi-center validation is proposed as future work
target_learners: potentially other healthcare professional groups such as nursing or emergency medicine students
target_learning_goals: Theoretical knowledge of first aid for traumatic dental injuries, including crown fracture management and tooth avulsion response
examples: Administered as an anonymous questionnaire during classes to 290 medical students at Poznan University of Medical Sciences, with scores summed to a maximum of 63 points and converted to a percentage
key_sources: Pawlaczyk-Kamieńska T, Jastrzębski B, Kamieńska P, Kamieńska W, Marushko O, Marushko O, Kruszyńska D. (2025). The evaluation of declarative and objective knowledge of first aid for dental traumatic injuries among medical students: development and validation of a competency assessment tool. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08153-z

article_title: Optimizing cost-effectiveness in remote objective structured clinical examinations through targeted double scoring methodologies.
citation: Fu Zhihui, Wu Yuhong, Xu Lingling, Cai Fen, Liu Ren, Jiang Zhehan. (2025). Optimizing cost-effectiveness in remote objective structured clinical examinations through targeted double scoring methodologies. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2025.2467477
title: Four-step TDS decision workflow: initial scoring, CSR check, conditional second rating, and final-score combination
description: This pattern specifies the operational sequence TDS uses for each examinee at each station. As summarized in the article's flowchart, "(1) Initial Scoring: Rater 1 evaluated the examinee's performance and assigns a score", then a decision point checks whether that score falls within the CSR; "If the score is outside the CSR, no double scoring is needed, else, Rater 2 was invited to evaluate the examinee's performance"; and if double scoring was applied, the two scores were combined (e.g., averaged) as the final score, otherwise the Rater 1 score stands. The pattern localizes extra rating effort at the task/station level where pass/fail risk is highest.
requirements: A rater pool with expertise labels so that raters only rate performances matching their professional strengths, with Rater 1 randomly assigned to ensure unbiased initial scoring.
constraints: Station-level (rather than overall-score) CSR decisions complicate analysis because many per-examinee combinations of double-scored and singly-scored tasks emerge.
The study assumed an overall OSCE score is formed by combining station scores, e.g., by adding them.
target_learners: clinical medicine undergraduates in remote OSCE assessments
target_learning_goals: accurate and cost-efficient pass/fail classification of clinical skills performance
examples: In the study's flowchart, scores outside the CSR used the Rater 1 score directly, while scores inside the CSR were averaged across Rater 1 and Rater 2.
key_sources: Fu Zhihui, Wu Yuhong, Xu Lingling, Cai Fen, Liu Ren, Jiang Zhehan. (2025). Optimizing cost-effectiveness in remote objective structured clinical examinations through targeted double scoring methodologies. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2025.2467477
grain_size: assessment/scoring-assignment level (per task or station per examinee)

article_title: Opening Pandora's box - key facilitators of practice change in detecting and responding to childhood adversity - a practitioner perspective.
citation: Loveday Sarah, Chen Lingling, Constable Leanne N., Kabir Ashraful, White Natalie, Goldfeld Sharon, Sanci Lena, Hiscock Harriet. (2024). Opening Pandora's box - key facilitators of practice change in detecting and responding to childhood adversity - a practitioner perspective. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-024-04918-5
title: Theoretical Domains Framework and COM-B model used to identify drivers of and barriers to practitioner practice change
description: The study used the Theoretical Domains Framework, which "integrates and simplifies 33 theories of behaviour change into a framework with 14 domains", linked to the COM-B model in which behaviour results from interactions between capability, opportunity and motivation. Themes from the qualitative analysis were mapped onto TDF domains and COM-B: facilitators mapped to 'social influence', 'knowledge', 'belief about capabilities' and 'behavioural regulation', and barriers to 'environmental context and resources' and 'emotion'. The article notes no themes mapped to physical capability, psychological capability being more important for driving practice change.
requirements: Themes from qualitative analysis are cross-referenced with the TDF domains to determine the most important facilitators and barriers
constraints: No domains were significantly endorsed by practitioners, which the authors say demonstrates the complexity of identifying the key factors for changing behaviour
target_learning_goals: identifying and responding to childhood adversity in clinical and social care encounters
examples: Themes from 21 practitioner interviews were mapped onto TDF domains and COM-B in Table 5, with 'emotion' mapped to the Opening Pandora's Box barrier theme.
key_sources: Loveday Sarah, Chen Lingling, Constable Leanne N., Kabir Ashraful, White Natalie, Goldfeld Sharon, Sanci Lena, Hiscock Harriet. (2024). Opening Pandora's box - key facilitators of practice change in detecting and responding to childhood adversity - a practitioner perspective. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-024-04918-5

article_title: Behaviours that prompt primary school teachers to adopt and implement physically active learning: a meta synthesis of qualitative evidence.
citation: Daly-Smith Andrew, Morris Jade L., Norris Emma, Williams Toni L., Archbold Victoria, Kallio Jouni, Tammelin Tuija H., Singh Amika, Mota Jorge, von Seelen Jesper, Pesce Caterina, Salmon Jo, McKay Heather, Bartholomew John, Resaland Geir Kare. (2021). Behaviours that prompt primary school teachers to adopt and implement physically active learning: a meta synthesis of qualitative evidence. International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-021-01221-9
title: TDF-aligned framework of teacher-level, school-level and external determinants of PAL implementation
description: The article organises its meta-synthesis findings into a theory-driven framework mapping seven themes and 31 sub-themes onto the Theoretical Domains Framework of behaviour change. The TDF is described as deriving "from 33 cross-disciplinary theories and 128 key theoretical behavioural constructs" and comprising 14 domains. The synthesis aligned ten of these domains to teachers' adoption and implementation of physically active learning, positioning educators' target behaviours to inform PAL teacher training programmes.
requirements: Themes and sub-themes were only mapped to a TDF domain when the text explicitly mentioned characteristics of that domain, and only for teacher behaviour, not pupil behaviour
constraints: Four TDF domains (Optimism, Intentions, Behavioural Regulation, Memory/Attention/Decision Processes) did not align with the findings and their influence may only emerge as PAL programmes develop
target_learning_goals: adopting and implementing physically active learning in curricular lessons
examples: The synthesis mapped themes such as PAL benefits, beliefs about capabilities, training, delivery, resources, whole-school approach and external factors to TDF domains in Table 2

article_title: The Effects of Doctoral Teaching Development on Early-Career STEM Scholars' College Teaching Self-efficacy.
citation: Connolly, M. R., Lee, Y.-G., & Savoy, J. N. (2018). The Effects of Doctoral Teaching Development on Early-Career STEM Scholars' College Teaching Self-efficacy. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-02-0039
title: Design doctoral teaching development so participants accrue more than 30–50 hours of engagement for practically meaningful self-efficacy gains
description: The article recommends attending to the dosage of TD, reporting that "more than 30–40 hours of engagement in TD would lead to significant gains in college teaching self-efficacy, especially in course planning and teaching methods," while low engagement below roughly 20–30 hours has little effect. Implications advise programs to organize and market TD so doctoral students can reach sufficient engagement, and to connect time spent to returns on investment to gain buy-in from students and advisors.
requirements: Programs must offer enough coordinated, sustained TD opportunities for participants to accumulate the higher engagement thresholds
constraints: The threshold question is correlational; the authors state whether there is a threshold or tipping point "must be studied further" and the estimate rests on observational data
examples: Graduate schools organizing TD into coherent frameworks such as Michigan State University's PREP program; national efforts including CIRTL and the Council of Graduate Schools' Preparing Future Faculty program
key_sources: Connolly, M. R., Lee, Y.-G., & Savoy, J. N. (2018). The Effects of Doctoral Teaching Development on Early-Career STEM Scholars' College Teaching Self-efficacy. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.17-02-0039

article_title: Enhancing communication skills for telehealth: development and implementation of a Teach-Back intervention for a national maternal and child health helpline in Australia.
citation: Morony Suzanne, Weir Kristie, Duncan Gregory, Biggs Janice, Nutbeam Don, Mccaffery Kirsten J. (2018). Enhancing communication skills for telehealth: development and implementation of a Teach-Back intervention for a national maternal and child health helpline in Australia. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-2956-6
title: Theoretical Domains Framework-guided intervention design for Teach-Back implementation
description: The article used the Theoretical Domains Framework and a model for developing theory-informed implementation interventions to map barriers (time, knowledge, skills, beliefs) and enablers (self-reflection, supportive work environment) onto intervention components. It examined "what (and whose) behaviours need to change; which barriers and enablers need to be addressed; which intervention components could respond to the barriers and enablers". Each barrier was assigned TDF domains and matched techniques, modes and content, e.g. role play facing away from each other to simulate the telephone environment.
requirements: Requires identifying the target behaviour and mapping barriers and enablers to theoretical domains before selecting intervention components
constraints: Training was limited to a maximum of two hours face-to-face in small groups at the helpline
target_learners: experienced maternal and child health telenurses
target_learning_goals: using the Teach-Back method to confirm caller understanding in telephone consultations
examples: Barriers such as time constraints were addressed by temporarily relaxing call duration guidelines and discussing that Teach-Back often reduced consultation time

Enhancing communication skills for telehealth: development and implementation of a Teach-Back intervention for a national maternal and child health helpline in Australia. article_title: Learning curves, taking instructions, and patient safety: using a theoretical domains framework in an interview study to investigate prescribing errors among trainee doctors.
citation: Duncan Eilidh M, Francis Jill J, Johnston Marie, Davey Peter, Maxwell Simon, McKay Gerard A, McLay James, Ross Sarah, Ryan Cristín, Webb David J, Bond Christine. (2012). Learning curves, taking instructions, and patient safety: using a theoretical domains framework in an interview study to investigate prescribing errors among trainee doctors. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/1748-5908-7-86
title: Theoretical Domains Framework: determinants of healthcare professionals' behavior clustered into 12 domains
description: The Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) is a framework from health psychology built from 33 behavioral theories, proposing that “determinants of healthcare professionals’ behavior cluster into 12 domains” such as social influences, behavioral regulation, and social/professional role and identity. This study used it to structure interview topic guides and coding categories for investigating prescribing errors among trainee doctors, ensuring a wide range of possible theoretical explanations was considered rather than a restricted set from individual theories.
requirements: Application requires specifying the behavior under investigation as a preliminary step, balancing precise specification against clinical usefulness and generalizability
constraints: The framework is not a theory, as it does not propose relationships between its elements
target_learners: postgraduate trainee doctors (foundation doctors) in hospitals
examples: A TDF-based semistructured topic guide prompted trainee doctors to discuss beliefs about prescribing and prescribing errors, with no new data generated by a final coverage prompt
key_sources: Duncan Eilidh M, Francis Jill J, Johnston Marie, Davey Peter, Maxwell Simon, McKay Gerard A, McLay James, Ross Sarah, Ryan Cristín, Webb David J, Bond Christine. (2012). Learning curves, taking instructions, and patient safety: using a theoretical domains framework in an interview study to investigate prescribing errors among trainee doctors.
